title: Critical Thinking · Episode 3
chapters: Regression to the mean: why extremes don't last
Science or pseudoscience? How to tell the difference

units.t: Critical Thinking. Episode three.
In this episode: How statistics can mislead, Regression to the mean: why extremes don't last, How to judge a claim and Science or pseudoscience? How to tell the difference.
Part one. How statistics can mislead.
The numbers can be true and still tell a false story.
Here's how to spot the tricks.
Averages and extremes.
Most misleading statistics aren't lies; the numbers are accurate.
The deception is in what's included, what's left out, how it's compared and how it's shown.
The 1954 book How to Lie with Statistics by Darrell Huff became a bestseller because its tricks were so common.
Most still are.
The 'average' usually means the mean: add everything up and divide.
But extremes drag the mean around.
If a billionaire walks into a café, the mean wealth of the customers soars, though nobody else got richer.
The median, the middle value when everything is lined up, is often more representative for skewed data like incomes and house prices.
When someone quotes an average, ask which one.
Percentages and pictures.
If an interest rate rises from 4% to 5%, that's one percentage point but a 25% increase.
If support for something rises from 10% to 15%, that's 5 percentage points, or a 50% increase.
Both are correct, and people choose whichever sounds more impressive.
A 200% increase in something rare might mean going from 1 case to 3.
Graphs mislead too.
The classic trick is a truncated y-axis: starting at 95 instead of 0 makes a small change look like a leap.
A convenient start and end date can make a trend look up or down.
Two lines on different scales can seem connected.
Check the axis labels, starting point and timeframe before reacting.
Who is missing.
A statistic is only as good as its sample.
Online polls anyone can vote in attract people with strong opinions and can be flooded by campaigns.
In 1936, the Literary Digest polled millions, drawing largely on car owners and telephone directories, and predicted a landslide defeat for Roosevelt.
He won by a landslide.
A well-designed random sample of around 1,000 is usually far more accurate than a huge biased one.
Survivorship bias is similar.
In World War II, the US military studied returning bombers to decide where to add armour.
Statistician Abraham Wald noted they only saw planes that survived: the areas without holes, like the engines, were where hits brought planes down.
Studying only successful businesses or old buildings still standing makes the same mistake.
Simpson's paradox.
Sometimes a trend that appears in every subgroup reverses when the data is combined.
In a well-known 1973 case, the University of California, Berkeley appeared to admit men at a higher rate than women overall.
But when researchers looked department by department, women were admitted at similar or higher rates in most departments.
The overall gap arose because women applied more often to highly competitive departments.
The lesson: how data is grouped can completely change its story.
Questions to ask.
When you meet a striking statistic, ask: Who collected it, and do they have an agenda?
How was the sample chosen, and how big was it?
Is it an average, and which kind?
Is it a relative or absolute change?
Compared with what, and over what time period?
What's left out?
Reputable sources, like the Australian Bureau of Statistics, publish their methods so you can check.
You don't need to be a mathematician to ask good questions about numbers.
The key idea: Accurate statistics can still mislead, and the median is often more representative than the mean when data is skewed.
Part two. Regression to the mean: why extremes don't last.
A footballer has a dream season, then a so-so one.
A new treatment seems to cure your worst week.
Often the real cause is a quiet statistical force.
The flight instructors.
The psychologist Daniel Kahneman told of teaching Israeli air force flight instructors.
One objected that praise works better than punishment.
When he praised an excellent manoeuvre, he said, the next attempt was usually worse.
When he shouted at a bad one, the next was usually better.
Kahneman realised the instructor saw something real but drew the wrong conclusion.
An unusually good flight is partly skill and partly luck, and luck tends not to repeat.
So the next attempt is likely to be closer to average, whatever the instructor says.
The same goes for unusually bad flights.
The praise and shouting were mostly irrelevant.
This pattern is called regression to the mean.
Skill plus luck.
Think of any performance as skill plus luck.
Skill is fairly stable.
Luck bounces around randomly.
When you pick out an extreme result, the very best or worst, you are partly selecting for skill and partly for unusually good or bad luck.
Next time the skill remains, but the luck is likely to be more ordinary, so the result moves back towards typical.
Crucially, no cause is needed.
Nobody got lazy or complacent.
The more luck matters, the stronger the pull to average.
Pure skill wouldn't regress; pure luck would regress completely.
Francis Galton noticed it in the 1880s: very tall parents tended to have tall children, but on average not quite as tall.
It describes groups, not destiny.
Curses and jinxes.
People joke about the Sports Illustrated cover jinx: athletes on the American magazine's cover often seem to slump soon after.
Similar talk follows big award winners and players who sign large contracts.
But think about when someone lands on a cover.
It is usually after a remarkable stretch, often their best ever, which almost certainly involved some good luck.
The following season is likely to be closer to their usual level, which looks like a slump by comparison.
No curse required.
The same logic applies to businesses praised after a record year, fund managers who topped the charts and restaurants that have just won an award.
Picking people at their peak practically guarantees an apparent decline afterwards.
Medicine and control groups.
When are you most likely to try a new remedy for back pain, a headache or a cold?
Usually when symptoms are at their worst.
Many conditions naturally fluctuate, so after a bad patch things are likely to improve somewhat, whatever you do.
If you took a remedy at the peak, it will seem to have worked.
That is a major reason researchers use control groups.
In a well designed trial, some patients get the treatment and others get a placebo or standard care, and both groups are chosen in the same way.
Regression affects both equally, so only a genuine difference between them shows a real effect.
This is general information, so speak to a health professional about your own situation.
Blackspots and big claims.
Imagine cameras installed at the intersections with the most crashes last year.
Next year, crashes there fall.
Success?
Partly, perhaps.
But some sites topped the list through an unusually unlucky year and would have improved anyway.
Road safety researchers account for this by comparing treated sites with similar untreated ones, or by using several years of data.
The trap also appears in schools, where extra help goes to the lowest scorers, and in workplaces, where struggling teams get a new manager.
So when something is chosen for being extreme, expect it to look less extreme next time, and ask what would have happened without the intervention.
Kahneman's instructors weren't wrong about what they saw, only about why.
The key idea: Praise seemed to make pilots worse and criticism seemed to make them better.
Part three. How to judge a claim.
'Scientists say…', 'A study found…'.
A practical checklist for deciding what to believe.
Not all evidence is equal.
Anecdotes, expert opinions, single studies and large reviews all count as 'evidence', but they're not equally reliable.
Personal stories and opinions sit near the bottom.
Above them come observational studies, then randomised controlled trials.
Near the top are systematic reviews and meta-analyses, which combine many good studies.
One study rarely settles a question.
Small studies can also produce dramatic results by chance.
Getting 7 heads in 10 coin flips isn't unusual; 7,000 heads in 10,000 flips would be astonishing.
A treatment that 'worked for 8 of 10 people' is far less convincing than one tested on thousands.
Surprising small-study findings often shrink in larger studies, the decline effect.
Compared with what.
Without a comparison group, you can't tell whether an improvement came from the treatment, the placebo effect or people simply getting better on their own.
The choice of comparison matters too.
A new drug that beats a sugar pill may still be worse than the treatment doctors already use, so the most useful trials test new options against standard care.
Be wary of comparisons with patients from years earlier, or with people who chose not to take part, since they may differ in many ways.
When you read about a study, ask: compared with what?
Risk needs numbers.
'Doubles your risk' sounds alarming, but if risk goes from 1 in 100,000 to 2 in 100,000, the absolute change is tiny.
Headlines prefer relative numbers because they sound bigger.
'Cuts risk by 50%' might mean 2 in 1,000 falling to 1 in 1,000.
Always ask: out of how many people?
Rarity also matters.
Imagine a disease affecting 1 in 1,000 people and a test that's 99% accurate.
Test 1,000 people: about 1 has the disease and tests positive, but about 10 of the 999 healthy people also test positive by mistake.
A positive result means only about a 1 in 11 chance of having it.
That's why doctors often confirm with a second test.
Who says so.
Ask who's making the claim and what they gain if you believe it.
Research funded by companies with a stake isn't automatically wrong, but it's more likely to favour the sponsor, so independent confirmation matters.
Be wary of claims that appear only on sites selling a product.
Is the source a peer-reviewed journal, a reputable organisation like the CSIRO or a university, or a press release, blog or social post?
Astronomer Carl Sagan popularised the principle that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.
Be alert to miracle breakthroughs, 'what they don't want you to know', testimonials instead of data, attacks on mainstream experts and pressure to buy now.
Real breakthroughs are usually cautious and replicated by independent teams.
A quick checklist.
Next time you meet a claim, run through six questions.
What's the source, and could they be biased?
What kind of evidence is it: anecdote, observational study or trial?
How many people were studied?
Compared with what?
What are the absolute numbers?
And what do most experts in the field think?
You won't always have time to check everything, but even asking two or three of these questions will make you far harder to fool.
The key idea: Evidence has a hierarchy, and small studies can produce dramatic results by chance, so the weight of evidence matters more than any single study.
Part four. Science or pseudoscience? How to tell the difference.
Astrology, crystal healing and a revolutionary new diet can all sound scientific.
A few sharp questions reveal which ideas are willing to be proven wrong.
Popper and falsifiability.
In Vienna after the First World War, young Karl Popper was surrounded by bold ideas.
Einstein's relativity made a risky prediction: starlight passing the Sun should bend by a specific amount.
In 1919, expeditions led by Arthur Eddington measured starlight during a solar eclipse and supported Einstein.
The theory could have failed, and it didn't.
Some popular theories of psychology and history, by contrast, explained every possible outcome.
Popper saw that as a weakness.
His answer to the problem of separating science from non-science was falsifiability.
'All swans are white' is falsifiable: one black swan breaks it, and Europeans found black swans in Western Australia.
'Invisible fairies tend my garden but leave no trace' isn't.
Falsifiable doesn't mean false, just testable.
Ask what would prove an idea wrong.
The warning signs.
Pseudoscience is dressed up to look scientific without behaving like science.
It shows familiar warning signs.
Claims are vague, so they can't easily be checked.
Evidence comes mainly from testimonials and anecdotes rather than controlled studies.
Scientific words such as 'quantum', 'energy' and 'frequency' are borrowed for glamour without precise meaning.
When a test fails, excuses appear: the sceptic's negative energy interfered.
The idea hasn't changed for decades despite new evidence.
Critics are dismissed as closed-minded.
And there is often something to buy.
No single sign proves an idea is bogus, but when several appear together, look much more carefully before you believe or spend.
Astrology under test.
Astrology makes claims that can, in principle, be tested: your birth chart is said to reveal your personality.
In a 1985 study in the journal Nature, physicist Shawn Carlson ran a double-blind test with astrologers who had agreed to the method in advance.
They were given birth charts and asked to match each to the correct personality profile from a small set of options.
Their success rate was about what guessing would produce.
Other studies have looked for links between star signs and personality or career and generally found nothing meaningful.
Astrology can still be enjoyable, a prompt for reflection or a bit of fun.
But as a scientific claim about how people work, it hasn't passed the test.
Homeopathy in Australia.
Homeopathy was developed in Germany around 1800 by Samuel Hahnemann.
Its central idea is that a substance causing symptoms can cure similar symptoms when heavily diluted, and that more dilution makes it stronger.
Many remedies are diluted so far that, statistically, not one molecule of the original substance is likely to remain.
In 2015, Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council published a major review of the evidence.
It concluded there were no health conditions for which there was reliable evidence that homeopathy was effective.
The council warned that choosing it over proven treatments may put health at risk.
This is general information rather than medical advice.
Talk to a doctor, and healthdirect is a reliable starting point for health questions in Australia.
Self-correction, not Galileo.
Science gets things wrong all the time.
What makes it different is that it has ways of finding and fixing errors.
Studies are checked by experts, results are repeated by independent teams, and failed ideas are revised or dropped.
For decades, doctors thought stomach ulcers were mainly caused by stress.
Perth researchers Barry Marshall and Robin Warren showed that a bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, played a central role.
Marshall even swallowed a culture to prove the point.
Doctors were sceptical, but evidence won, and the pair received the 2005 Nobel Prize.
Fringe promoters often say 'they laughed at Galileo'.
But for every rejected idea later proven right, vast numbers were rejected because they were wrong.
Galileo was vindicated by his observations, not by being mocked.
Being an outsider is fine.
Avoiding tests isn't.
The key idea: A claim is scientific if some observation could show it to be false, so a theory that fits every possible result tells you nothing.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why are median house prices usually reported instead of the mean?
Answer. A few extreme sales skew the mean.
Question two. Why did the flight instructor's criticism seem to work?
Answer. Poor flights were usually followed by average ones.
Question three. Which kind of evidence is generally the most reliable?
Answer. A systematic review of many studies.
Question four. What makes a claim scientific, according to falsifiability?
Answer. A test could show it to be false.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
